clue.text: Spirit embodied by secular Magna Carta

indicators.note: to be embodied by something is to be given a body that wraps right round you, so the letters sit inside the words that follow

parts.note: the tail of seculAR runs straight into MAGNA and picks up the C of Carta

explanation.walkthrough: The join between two words is where a hidden run is easiest to spot, and this one crosses three, which is why the constitutional surface holds together so well.
explanation.definitionFit: Spirit -> ARMAGNAC: definition by example, since Armagnac is one particular Gascon brandy rather than a synonym for spirits.

clue.text: Roguish Austen hero undressed Elizabeth finally

indicators.note: a word with its clothes off has lost the letters at each end, the ones that were covering the rest
what happens finally happens at the end, so only the closing letter of the name is wanted

parts.note: the Austen hero is Darcy, and undressed he keeps only his middle
Darcy's match ends in H, and that is all she contributes

explanation.walkthrough: Pride and Prejudice supplies both halves, so the clue reads as gossip about the novel rather than as two instructions.
explanation.definitionFit: Roguish -> ARCH: an arch smile is a knowing, mischievous one, the sense that survives in 'arch look' rather than the doorway or the chief-villain prefix.

clue.text: Trashing contents of Petit Trianon, mean European princess

indicators.note: trash a room and nothing is left where it stood, which is what happens to letters told to move
the contents are what you find once the container is off, so the outside letters at each end are dropped

parts.note: the queen's own little chateau at Versailles, giving up its outer P and N
four more letters, taken as they stand
E is the standard abbreviation for European

explanation.walkthrough: The Petit Trianon was her private retreat in the grounds of Versailles, so surface and letters are drawn from the same place.
explanation.definitionFit: princess -> MARIE ANTOINETTE: she was an archduchess of Austria and a princess of the house of Habsburg long before Versailles.

clue.text: When spread, marge's so light

indicators.note: marge is a spread, and spreading a thing pushes it out of the shape it arrived in - the letters go the same way

parts.note: eight letters including the possessive S, and nothing is added or thrown away

explanation.walkthrough: Marge is margarine and spreading is what you do with it, so the instruction hides inside an entirely sensible sentence about a tub.
explanation.definitionFit: light -> GOSSAMER: both are adjectives for something almost weightless, gossamer being the cobweb-fine kind of light rather than the opposite of dark.

clue.text: Car crash south of Aleppo cleared arterial route

indicators.note: a cleared building keeps its walls and loses everything inside, and a cleared word keeps its first and last letters
south is downwards on a map and downwards in a down entry, so this piece is written underneath the other

parts.note: clear the inside out of Aleppo and the two letters at the ends survive
RTA is a road traffic accident, the police shorthand for a car crash

explanation.walkthrough: RTA off a police report is the abbreviation worth banking here; the Syrian city keeps the sentence sounding like a news bulletin.
explanation.definitionFit: arterial route -> AORTA: an arterial road is a town's main road, and the aorta is the body's own main artery, so the phrase works in both anatomies.

clue.text: Uncover Blue River island figure revered along the Nile

parts.note: the Blue River is the Danube of the waltz, and uncovered it loses its D and its E

indicators.note: taking the cover off a word means stripping the letters at each end, the ones wrapped round the rest

parts.note: Is. is the map-maker's abbreviation for island

explanation.walkthrough: Blue and River belong to one name rather than two hints, and spotting Strauss's waltz behind them is the step that opens the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: figure revered along the Nile -> ANUBIS: the jackal-headed god of embalming, worshipped the length of ancient Egypt, so 'figure' means deity.

clue.text: Hunter set up sleeping accommodation at home

indicators.note: this is a down entry, so a piece stood on end climbs the grid and arrives with its letters in the opposite order

parts.note: a dorm is a room full of beds, sleeping accommodation in one word
someone at home is in, the crossword's hardest-working two letters

explanation.walkthrough: Nimrod is the mighty hunter of Genesis, which is also why Elgar called a friend's variation by his name.
explanation.definitionFit: Hunter -> NIMROD: the great-grandson of Noah described in Genesis as a mighty hunter, and since then the word for any keen hunter.

clue.text: Robin Day worked with braille books here

definitions.note: 'books here' points at the answer as a place rather than offering a noun you could swap in: the setter defines it by what it holds and where, which is fair for a building.

indicators.note: dough is worked until nothing of its old shape is left, and the same is being asked of these letters

parts.note: Sir Robin Day, the BBC's great interrogator, hands over the eight letters of his name
the raised-dot reading system joins the pile whole, seven letters more

explanation.walkthrough: 'Day worked with braille' reads as a career and a cause rather than as fifteen letters, which is what keeps the anagram out of sight.
explanation.definitionFit: books here -> BODLEIAN LIBRARY: Oxford's copyright library, entitled to a copy of every book published in Britain, so 'here' is where books genuinely are.

clue.text: Seated, eating cold Japanese noodles over US city

indicators.note: whatever is eaten ends up inside the eater, so these letters are swallowed by the word beside them

parts.note: seated is sat, and it opens up to take the meal
C is the letter on the cold tap
ramen are the Japanese noodles
O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over

explanation.walkthrough: Cricket's O for an over is the convention to keep; the restaurant scene is doing all the misdirection on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: US city -> SACRAMENTO: California's state capital on the river of the same name, so the phrase names one city by example.

clue.text: Well wrapped up, son walked with clumsy gait

parts.note: S is the family-tree abbreviation for son
to waddle is to walk with the rolling, ungainly gait of a duck

explanation.walkthrough: 'Well wrapped up' sounds like advice about cold weather, which is exactly what hides the baby in its swaddling clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Well wrapped up -> SWADDLED: the word for an infant bound snugly in strips of cloth, so the everyday phrase describes that binding.

clue.text: Irish city's ship's company that gets stuck into the vino

definitions.text: that gets stuck into the vino
definitions.note: The answer is defined by what it does rather than by a noun you could swap in, and the joke is that what it really gets stuck into is the cork rather than the wine.

parts.note: Cork is the city on the Lee, and the possessive S it owns comes along as a letter
a ship's company is its crew

explanation.walkthrough: Cork's own name is the joke: the Irish city and the thing in the bottleneck are the same word, and only one of them is doing the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: that gets stuck into the vino -> CORKSCREW: the spiral is driven into the cork of a wine bottle, so 'gets stuck in' is meant literally.

clue.text: Peninsula: sea freezing cold

parts.note: the Med is the sea, shortened the way everyone shortens it
water freezes at nought degrees, and nought is written as the letter O
C is the abbreviation for cold, and for Celsius on the same thermometer

explanation.walkthrough: Freezing cold is 0C on a thermometer, which is the joke the last two letters are built on.
explanation.definitionFit: Peninsula -> MEDOC: the tongue of land north of Bordeaux between the Gironde estuary and the Atlantic, better known for its clarets than its shape.

clue.text: Source of protein, iron? Thanks!

parts.note: Fe is iron's symbol on the periodic table
ta is the everyday British thanks

explanation.walkthrough: Two of the most reliable abbreviations in the game sit side by side, and the exclamation mark makes them read as chat rather than chemistry.
explanation.definitionFit: Source of protein -> FETA: the Greek sheep's-milk cheese, an example of a protein food rather than a synonym, which is what the question mark signals.

clue.text: Group of stars departs capital in open landau

indicators.note: a landau with its top open is a carriage you can see straight into, and a word opened this way gives up what is inside it
the plainest instruction there is for putting one thing within another

parts.note: opened up, LANDAU parts with the L and U at its ends
D is the timetable's abbreviation for departs
the capital wanted is Italy's

explanation.walkthrough: D for departs comes straight off a railway board, and 'capital' asks for a city rather than a capital letter: two habits worth keeping.
explanation.definitionFit: Group of stars -> ANDROMEDA: the constellation named for the chained princess of Greek myth, so one named constellation answers the general phrase.

clue.text: Where to see Stanley, Bill and Charlie call Tony endlessly?

indicators.note: something endless has had its end removed, so the final letter of the name goes

parts.note: a bill is an account, written a/c
Charlie is C in the radio alphabet
to call someone is to ring them
Tony without his last letter stops at TON

explanation.walkthrough: Bill, Charlie and Tony read as three blokes in a pub and are really three separate conventions, which is the whole disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: Where to see Stanley -> ACCRINGTON: Accrington Stanley are the Lancashire league club, so the town is where that Stanley plays.

clue.text: Sweeper coached away from the ball?

definitions.text: Sweeper coached away from the ball?

parts.note: not the defender playing behind the back four, which is how the football surface reads it: this sweeper works a broom round a hearth full of ashes
'coached' is transport rather than training - a pumpkin turned into a carriage - and 'the ball' is the palace dance that has to be left by midnight

explanation.walkthrough: Every word carries a football reading and a pantomime one at the same time, and the question mark is the setter admitting the whole sentence is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweeper coached away from the ball? -> the fairy-tale girl who sweeps the cinders, rides to the dance by coach and must leave it at midnight.

clue.text: Each second flood covers small part of Manhattan

indicators.note: to cover a thing is to lie over it on both sides, so the letter covered ends up in the middle

parts.note: ea. is the price-list shorthand for each
S is the clock's abbreviation for a second
the flood tide is the incoming one, so flood alone gives TIDE
S is the size on a small label

explanation.walkthrough: Manhattan's East Side is named by compass point, and the rising water of the surface is what keeps three abbreviations from looking like abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: part of Manhattan -> EAST SIDE: the strip of the island east of Central Park, so the definition names a district rather than translating a word.

clue.text: Best-loved shanty town bulldozing large area

indicators.note: a bulldozer flattens what stands there and clears it off the site, so the letters it names are taken away

parts.note: a favela is a Brazilian shanty town
L for large and A for area, the two letters flattened out of the favela

explanation.walkthrough: Fave is the teenage clipping of favourite, and the slum clearance in the surface is the setter's joke about which letters go.
explanation.definitionFit: Best-loved -> FAVE: the informal short form of favourite, and your favourite is by definition the one you love best.

clue.text: We're told Samuel's girlfriend abridged dissident literature

indicators.note: an abridged book has had its ending cut, and so has this word
being told a thing means meeting it by ear, so what matters is the sound and not the spelling

parts.note: Samuel shortens to Sam, and Sam's spoken aloud ends on a Z sound, written out as you hear it
a girlfriend is a date, and abridged she is DAT

explanation.walkthrough: Samizdat was writing the Soviet censor never saw: typed at home, copied by carbon paper and passed from hand to hand.
explanation.definitionFit: dissident literature -> SAMIZDAT: the Russian word for self-published banned writing circulated in secret, so it names that literature exactly.

clue.text: Cross and abusive on the phone

indicators.note: a voice down a line is all you get, so the word arrives as a sound with its spelling still to be guessed

parts.note: abusive means rude, and that word said aloud sounds identical to the differently-spelled word this clue wants

explanation.walkthrough: A rood is the great crucifix mounted above the chancel screen of an old church, so the definition is architectural rather than bad-tempered.
explanation.definitionFit: Cross -> ROOD: the church word for the crucifix over the screen, which is why parish churches have a rood loft and a rood screen.

clue.text: Where one might find old Reg Ford?

definitions.text: Where one might find old Reg Ford?

parts.note: reads as a bloke with a first name and a surname, which is the whole disguise: a reg is a registration plate and a Ford is the make wearing it
the question mark warns that a place is being described rather than named, and 'old' is what the motor trade politely prints as second-hand

explanation.walkthrough: Two ordinary trade words are wearing capital letters: Reg for the plate on the windscreen, Ford for the badge on the bonnet.
explanation.definitionFit: Where one might find old Reg Ford? -> the dealer's forecourt of second-hand motors, exactly where an ageing Ford still carrying its plate ends up.

clue.text: Novelist comfortable after spine drained

indicators.note: a drained tank has had everything inside emptied out and only its walls left standing
in a down entry after means further down the column, so this piece follows the one already made

parts.note: drain the middle out of SPINE and the two end letters are left
someone comfortable in themselves is well

explanation.walkthrough: Anna Sewell wrote Black Beauty and nothing else, so a bare 'Novelist' is doing a lot of work while the surface complains about a bad back.
explanation.definitionFit: Novelist -> SEWELL: Anna Sewell, author of Black Beauty, so the definition is answered by one novelist's name rather than by a synonym.

clue.text: Breaking news: poor Spooner being ostracised

indicators.note: a story that breaks arrives without warning and pushes whatever was scheduled out of its place, which is what these letters are told to do
someone in a poor way is not holding together, and letters in that state will not keep the order they came in

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for new, and crossword shorthand doubles a letter to make it plural, so news is two of them
the reverend hands over the seven letters of his surname, and they go straight into the pile

explanation.walkthrough: Spooner is wanted for his letters, not his manner of speech: nothing here asks you to swap any initial sounds, which is the trap his name always sets.
explanation.definitionFit: being ostracised -> NON-PERSON: someone struck off the official record and treated as never having existed, the Soviet practice Orwell wrote up as the unperson.

clue.text: Note buzz surrounding Alqosh's top prophet

indicators.note: what surrounds a thing closes on it from both sides, so the letters part company and the piece named goes between them
the top of a name is where it starts, so only its opening letter is wanted

parts.note: N is a note in music, one of the seven from A to G
a buzz is a hum
the opening letter of the Iraqi town's name

explanation.walkthrough: Alqosh in northern Iraq keeps the tomb traditionally said to be this prophet's, which is why that town and no other is in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: prophet -> NAHUM: one of the twelve minor prophets of the Hebrew Bible, so the answer is an instance of the word rather than a synonym.

clue.text: Foreign language starts to influence opinion around part of UK

indicators.note: the start of a word is the letter it begins with, and two words are being asked for theirs
a piece placed around another closes over it, so the letters part company to let it in

parts.note: the opening letters of influence and of opinion
GB is Great Britain, the part of the UK that leaves Northern Ireland out

explanation.walkthrough: 'Part of UK' is a precise description rather than a loose one: Great Britain really is a proper part of the United Kingdom.
explanation.definitionFit: Foreign language -> IGBO: the language of south-eastern Nigeria and one of that country's three largest, so the phrase names one tongue by example.

clue.text: County clerk gossiped

indicators.note: gossip travels by mouth and never in writing, so the word beside it reaches you as a sound with its spelling still to be settled

parts.note: a clerk is said 'clark' on this side of the Atlantic, and Clark is the mild-mannered reporter of the Daily Planet whose surname goes in the grid

explanation.walkthrough: Half a famous name is a standing invitation to supply the other half: a setter can write Sherlock for Holmes, or a spoken Clark for this one, with no further signal.
explanation.definitionFit: County -> KENT: an English county rather than a synonym, the south-eastern one known as the Garden of England.

clue.text: What idiot rejected cash meant for the church?

indicators.note: something rejected is thrown back at you, and letters thrown back are read from the far end

parts.note: eh? is what you say when you did not catch it - 'what' out loud
a tit is a mild British word for an idiot

explanation.walkthrough: A tithe was the tenth of a year's produce the parish took by law, so this is a historical levy rather than a collection plate.
explanation.definitionFit: cash meant for the church -> TITHE: the tenth part of income that the church could once claim by right, so the phrase names the levy itself.

clue.text: Heading back east late, he would dry out

indicators.note: heading back is retracing the way you came, and this is an across entry, so the letters are read right to left

parts.note: E is the compass abbreviation for east
late is tardy
he would contracts to he'd

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing is shuffled here: three pieces line up in clue order and the whole line is then read from the other end.
explanation.definitionFit: dry out -> DEHYDRATE: to dehydrate something is to drive the water out of it, which is the transitive sense 'dry out' carries.

clue.text: Make cross stitch using this?

definitions.meaning: this half asks for a verb meaning to keep picking at someone until they are cross
the implement the stitching is actually done with

explanation.walkthrough: The two halves are glued together by 'cross stitch', a real embroidery term that belongs to neither of them, and that join is the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Make cross -> NEEDLE means to provoke or irritate; stitch using this -> NEEDLE is the sewing implement itself, the two senses meeting in cross-stitch.

clue.text: Hot, steamy, lacking oxygen, turning violet

indicators.note: what a thing lacks it does not have, so the letter named next never joins the pile
milk turns and comes back as something else, and letters told to turn come back in another order

parts.note: nine letters of sauna to work from
oxygen is O on the periodic table, and that O is the letter dropped before the shuffle

explanation.walkthrough: Amethyst is the violet quartz, so 'turning violet' describes a colour change on the surface and a gemstone underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: violet -> AMETHYST: the stone is named for its violet colour, so a shade answers for the gem that is best known for wearing it.
